real-numbers.intro: Anu is in Class 10 now, and her board exam is a few months away. Thatha opens his old maths book and says, 'Every number you know is built from a few special bricks, the primes. Once you see the bricks, HCF, LCM and even √2 become easy.'
before: know what a prime number and a composite number are
find factors and multiples
know HCF and LCM from Class 7

lessons.title: Every number is made of prime bricks
lessons.story: Anu breaks 1,260 into factors: 1,260 = 4 × 315, then keeps breaking. Ravi starts with 1,260 = 35 × 36 instead. 'We started differently. Will we get different primes?'
text: Keep breaking each factor until only primes are left. Anu gets 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 × 7. Ravi gets exactly the same primes, only in a different order.

This is the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic: every composite number can be written as a product of primes, and this factorisation is unique, apart from the order of the primes. We write it with powers: 1,260 = 2² × 3² × 5 × 7.

picture.caption: 1,260 = 4 × 9 × 35 = 2² × 3² × 5 × 7. Every route gives the same primes.

think.question: Can 6ⁿ end with the digit 0 for any natural number n?
think.answer: No. A number ending in 0 is divisible by 10 = 2 × 5, so it needs the prime 5. 6ⁿ = 2ⁿ × 3ⁿ has no 5, and the factorisation is unique, so 5 can never appear.

lessons.aha: Every composite number is a product of primes in exactly one way. Use this to answer 'can it end in 0?' questions.

lessons.title: HCF and LCM from the prime bricks
lessons.story: Two traffic lights change every 84 seconds and every 90 seconds. Thatha asks: 'What is the largest number that divides both? And when do they change together?'
text: Write both numbers with prime powers: 84 = 2² × 3 × 7 and 90 = 2 × 3² × 5.

HCF: take only the primes they share, each with its smaller power: 2¹ × 3¹ = 6. LCM: take every prime that appears, each with its larger power: 2² × 3² × 5 × 7 = 1,260. The lights change together every 1,260 seconds, that is, every 21 minutes.

picture.caption: HCF: common primes, smaller powers. LCM: all primes, larger powers.

think.question: Find the HCF and LCM of 6, 72 and 120.

lessons.aha: HCF uses common primes with the smallest powers. LCM uses all primes with the largest powers.
formulas: HCF = product of common primes (smallest powers)
LCM = product of all primes (largest powers)

lessons.title: The HCF × LCM shortcut
lessons.story: Ravi says, 'The HCF of 26 and 91 is 13. I can find the LCM in one second.' How?
text: For any two positive integers a and b: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b. So LCM(26, 91) = 26 × 91 ÷ 13 = 182.
Careful: this rule works for two numbers only, not for three. Also, the HCF always divides the LCM. So HCF = 12 and LCM = 90 is impossible, because 12 does not divide 90.

picture.caption: The product rule is only for two numbers.

think.question: The HCF of two numbers is 18 and their product is 12,960. Find their LCM.

lessons.aha: HCF × LCM = product of the two numbers. The HCF always divides the LCM.
formulas: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b

lessons.title: Numbers that are not fractions
lessons.story: Thatha draws a square with sides of 1 m and its diagonal. 'By Pythagoras, the diagonal is √2 m. Try to write √2 as a fraction.' Anu tries 7/5 = 1.4 and 141/100 = 1.41, but neither squares to exactly 2.
text: A rational number can be written as p/q, where p and q are integers and q ≠ 0. A number that cannot be written this way is irrational: √2, √3, √5, π.
We need one fact from prime factorisation: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a. (The primes of a² are the primes of a, each used twice.)

picture.caption: The diagonal of a 1 × 1 square is √2. Swing it down to mark √2 on the number line.

think.question: If 3 divides n², must 3 divide n? Check with n = 6 and n = 7.
think.answer: Yes. 6² = 36 is divisible by 3 and so is 6. 7² = 49 is not divisible by 3, and neither is 7.

lessons.aha: Irrational numbers cannot be written as p/q. Key fact: if a prime p divides a², then p divides a.

lessons.title: Proving √2 is irrational
lessons.story: Ravi asks, 'How can anyone be sure that no fraction equals √2? There are infinitely many fractions!' Thatha smiles: 'We prove it by contradiction.'
text: Suppose √2 = a/b in lowest terms (a and b have no common factor except 1). Squaring: 2b² = a², so 2 divides a², and therefore 2 divides a. Write a = 2c.

Then 2b² = 4c², so b² = 2c². Now 2 divides b², so 2 divides b. But then 2 divides both a and b, which contradicts 'lowest terms'. So our assumption was wrong: √2 is irrational. The same steps prove √3 and √5 irrational.

picture.caption: Proof by contradiction, in four steps.

think.question: In the proof for √5, which prime replaces 2?
think.answer: 5: 5b² = a², so 5 divides a; write a = 5c; then b² = 5c², so 5 divides b.

lessons.aha: To prove √p irrational: assume a/b in lowest terms, show p divides both a and b, and reach a contradiction.

lessons.title: Irrational expressions like 3 + 2√5
lessons.story: The board paper says: 'Given that √5 is irrational, prove that 3 + 2√5 is irrational.' Anu panics. Thatha says, 'Use the same trick, but it is much shorter.'
text: Assume 3 + 2√5 = r, a rational number. Then √5 = (r − 3)/2. The right side is rational (rationals are closed under −, × and ÷ by non-zero numbers). So √5 would be rational, which is false. Hence 3 + 2√5 is irrational.
Rules: rational + irrational = irrational, and non-zero rational × irrational = irrational. But irrational + irrational can be rational: √2 + (−√2) = 0.

picture.caption: Mixing a rational with an irrational keeps it irrational.

think.question: Is (√3 + 1)(√3 − 1) rational or irrational?

lessons.aha: Assume the expression is rational, solve for the root, and show the root would then be rational: a contradiction.

formulas: HCF(a, b) × LCM(a, b) = a × b
p prime, p | a² ⇒ p | a

polynomials.intro: Ravi throws a ball for his dog. The ball's height follows a smooth curve: up, then down to the ground. Thatha says, 'That curve is the graph of a polynomial. The moments when the height is zero are its zeroes, and the numbers in the polynomial tell you those moments without drawing anything.'
before: simplify algebraic expressions
factorise quadratic expressions by splitting the middle term
plot points on a graph

lessons.title: Polynomials and their degree
lessons.story: Anu sees three expressions on the board: 3x + 2, x² − 5x + 6 and 2x³ − x. 'Which is the odd one out?' asks Thatha.
text: A polynomial in x has terms of the form (number) × x^(whole number). Its degree is the highest power of x. 3x + 2 is linear (degree 1), x² − 5x + 6 is quadratic (degree 2), 2x³ − x is cubic (degree 3).
1/x, √x and x^(−2) are not allowed, so expressions like x + 1/x are not polynomials.

picture.caption: Only whole-number powers of x are allowed.

think.question: What is the degree of 5 − 4x + x²?

lessons.aha: The degree is the highest power of x. Degree 1, 2, 3: linear, quadratic, cubic.

lessons.title: A zero is where the graph meets the x-axis
lessons.story: Ravi's ball height is y = −x² + 2x + 3 (x in seconds). 'When is the ball on the ground?' Anu draws the graph.
text: A zero of p(x) is a number k with p(k) = 0. On the graph of y = p(x), a zero is an x-coordinate where the curve meets the x-axis.
Here −x² + 2x + 3 = −(x − 3)(x + 1), so the zeroes are 3 and −1. The curve cuts the x-axis exactly at x = −1 and x = 3. The ball lands at x = 3 seconds. The zero −1 is before the throw.

picture.caption: The graph cuts the x-axis at the zeroes, −1 and 3.

think.question: The graph of y = p(x) touches the x-axis at one point only. How many zeroes does p(x) have?
think.answer: One (the curve meets the x-axis only once).

lessons.aha: Number of zeroes = number of points where the graph meets the x-axis.
formulas: p(k) = 0 ⇔ k is a zero ⇔ (k, 0) is on the graph

lessons.title: How many zeroes can a quadratic have?
lessons.story: Thatha draws three cups (parabolas) at different heights. 'Count where each one meets the x-axis.'
text: The graph of y = ax² + bx + c is a parabola. It opens upward if a > 0 and downward if a < 0.

A quadratic polynomial can have two zeroes (cuts the axis twice), one zero (touches the axis) or no zero (stays above or below). A cubic polynomial has at most 3 zeroes. In general, a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes.

picture.caption: Two zeroes (x² − 4), one zero (touches at 2) and no zero (x² + 2).

think.question: Can a quadratic polynomial have 3 zeroes?
think.answer: No. A degree-2 polynomial has at most 2 zeroes.

lessons.aha: A polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes. A parabola can cut, touch or miss the x-axis.

lessons.title: The secret link: sum and product of zeroes
lessons.story: Anu factorises 2x² − 8x + 6 = 2(x − 1)(x − 3). The zeroes are 1 and 3. Thatha asks, 'Without factorising, can you get 4 and 3 from the numbers 2, −8 and 6?'
text: For p(x) = ax² + bx + c with zeroes α and β: α + β = −b/a and αβ = c/a.
Check: sum 1 + 3 = 4 = −(−8)/2 and product 1 × 3 = 3 = 6/2. ✓ Why does it work? ax² + bx + c = a(x − α)(x − β) = ax² − a(α + β)x + aαβ. Compare the coefficients.

picture.caption: The coefficients predict the sum and product of the zeroes.

think.question: Find the sum and product of the zeroes of 3x² − 7x + 2 without solving.

lessons.aha: Sum of zeroes = −b/a. Product of zeroes = c/a.

lessons.title: Building a polynomial from its zeroes
lessons.story: Thatha gives a challenge: 'Make a quadratic polynomial whose zeroes add to 4 and multiply to 1.'
text: If the sum is S and the product is P, then x² − Sx + P has these zeroes. Any multiple k(x² − Sx + P), with k ≠ 0, also works.
Sum 4, product 1 gives x² − 4x + 1. For zeroes −1/4 and 1/4: sum 0, product −1/16, so x² − 1/16, or 16x² − 1 (multiply by 16 to clear fractions).

steps: Multiply by k to clear fractions
picture.caption: From zeroes to polynomial.

think.question: Find a quadratic polynomial with zeroes 4 and −3.

lessons.aha: A quadratic with sum S and product P of zeroes is k(x² − Sx + P).

lessons.title: Using α and β without finding them
lessons.story: The question says: 'α and β are the zeroes of x² − 5x + 6. Find α² + β².' Ravi starts solving for α and β. Thatha says, 'There is a faster way.'
text: Use α + β = 5 and αβ = 6. Then α² + β² = (α + β)² − 2αβ = 25 − 12 = 13. And 1/α + 1/β = (α + β)/αβ = 5/6.
If one zero is given, substitute it to find an unknown coefficient: if 2 is a zero of x² + kx − 6, then 4 + 2k − 6 = 0 and k = 1.

linear-equations.intro: At the school fair, Anu buys 2 adult tickets and 3 student tickets for ₹390. Ravi buys 3 adult tickets and 2 student tickets for ₹410. 'Can we find the price of each ticket?' asks Anu. Two unknowns need two clues. That is what a pair of linear equations gives us.

plot points and draw a straight line on a graph

lessons.title: One equation, a whole line of answers
lessons.story: Anu writes one clue: 2a + 3s = 390. She tries a = 90, s = 70: it works. She tries a = 120, s = 50: it also works!
text: A linear equation in two variables, ax + by + c = 0, has infinitely many solutions. Each solution is a point (x, y), and all of them lie on one straight line.
One clue is not enough to fix the prices. A second clue gives a second line, and the answer is where the two lines meet.

picture.caption: Every solution of x + y = 5 lies on one straight line.

think.question: How many solutions does x + y = 7 have?
think.answer: Infinitely many; every point on its line.

lessons.aha: A linear equation in two variables is a straight line. Its solutions are all the points on the line.

lessons.title: Two lines: the graphical method
lessons.story: Thatha draws x + y = 5 and x − y = 1 on graph paper. The lines cross at one point.
text: The solution of the pair is the point that lies on both lines: their intersection. Here it is (3, 2): 3 + 2 = 5 and 3 − 2 = 1. ✓
To draw each line, make a small table of two or three points (for example, put x = 0 and y = 0), plot them and join.

picture.caption: The lines meet at (3, 2), the unique solution.

think.question: Two lines cross at (−1, 4). What is the solution of the pair?

lessons.aha: The solution of a pair of equations is the point where their lines meet.

lessons.title: Meet, never meet, or the same line
lessons.story: Ravi draws x + 2y = 4 and 2x + 4y = 9. 'My lines never meet!' Anu draws x + y = 3 and 2x + 2y = 6. 'Mine are the same line!'
text: Three things can happen. Intersecting lines: exactly one solution (consistent). Parallel lines: no solution (inconsistent). Coincident lines: infinitely many solutions (consistent, dependent).
You can decide without drawing. For a₁x + b₁y + c₁ = 0 and a₂x + b₂y + c₂ = 0, compare the ratios a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂ and c₁/c₂.

picture.caption: Compare the ratios of the coefficients.

think.question: For which k do kx + 3y = k − 3 and 12x + ky = k have no solution?
think.answer: k/12 = 3/k gives k = ±6. For k = −6, the c-ratio is (−9)/(−6) = 3/2, which is not −1/2. So k = −6. (For k = 6, all three ratios are 1/2: coincident.)

lessons.aha: Compare a₁/a₂, b₁/b₂, c₁/c₂ to know the number of solutions before solving.

lessons.title: The substitution method
lessons.story: Anu solves 2x + y = 7 and x − y = 2 without a graph.
text: From the simpler equation, write one variable in terms of the other: y = x − 2.
Substitute in the other equation: 2x + (x − 2) = 7, so 3x = 9 and x = 3. Then y = 3 − 2 = 1. Check in both equations: 6 + 1 = 7 ✓ and 3 − 1 = 2 ✓.

steps: Make y the subject: y = x − 2
picture.caption: Substitution: one variable at a time.

think.question: Solve x + y = 14 and x − y = 4 by substitution.

lessons.aha: Substitute one equation into the other to get one equation in one variable.

lessons.title: The elimination method
lessons.story: For the fair tickets, 2a + 3s = 390 and 3a + 2s = 410. Thatha says, 'Make one variable disappear.'
text: Multiply the equations so that one variable has equal coefficients: ×3 and ×2 give 6a + 9s = 1,170 and 6a + 4s = 820. Subtract: 5s = 350, so s = 70. Then 2a + 210 = 390, so a = 90.
Shortcut for this pair: adding gives 5a + 5s = 800 (a + s = 160) and subtracting gives a − s = 20. So a = 90, s = 70.

picture.caption: Elimination: remove one variable.

think.question: Solve 3x + 4y = 10 and 2x − 2y = 2 by elimination.
think.answer: Multiply the second by 2: 4x − 4y = 4; add: 7x = 14, x = 2, y = 1.

lessons.aha: Make the coefficients of one variable equal, then add or subtract to eliminate it.

quadratic-equations.intro: Anu's class wants a rectangular prayer hall with an area of 300 m². The length must be one metre more than twice the breadth. 'Let the breadth be x,' says Anu. 'Then x(2x + 1) = 300.' Ravi looks at the x². 'That is not a linear equation. How do we solve it?' This is a quadratic equation.
before: expand and factorise expressions like (x + 3)(x − 5)
find square roots
solve linear equations

lessons.title: What is a quadratic equation?
lessons.story: Anu writes the hall equation: x(2x + 1) = 300. She expands it: 2x² + x − 300 = 0.
text: A quadratic equation is an equation of the form ax² + bx + c = 0, where a, b, c are real numbers and a ≠ 0. The highest power of x is exactly 2.
Always expand and bring all terms to one side before you decide. (x + 2)² = x² + 3 gives 4x + 1 = 0: the x² cancels, so it is NOT quadratic.

picture.caption: Simplify first. A quadratic keeps an x² term with a ≠ 0.

think.question: Is x(x + 1) + 8 = (x + 2)(x − 2) quadratic?
think.answer: x² + x + 8 = x² − 4 gives x + 12 = 0. Not quadratic.

lessons.aha: Quadratic: ax² + bx + c = 0 with a ≠ 0. Simplify before you decide.

lessons.title: Solving by factorisation
lessons.story: Ravi tries 2x² + x − 300 = 0. Thatha says, 'Split the middle term. You need two numbers that multiply to 2 × (−300) = −600 and add to 1.'
text: If a product is zero, one factor is zero: 2x + 25 = 0 or x − 12 = 0. So x = −25/2 or x = 12. The breadth cannot be negative, so the breadth is 12 m and the length is 25 m.

arithmetic-progressions.intro: Anu saves ₹50 in the first week, ₹60 in the second, ₹70 in the third, and so on. 'How much will I save in week 20? And how much altogether?' The amounts go up by the same step every week. Such a list is an arithmetic progression.

lessons.title: Same step every time
lessons.story: Ravi climbs a staircase where each step is 15 cm higher than the one before. Heights from the floor: 15, 30, 45, 60, …
text: An arithmetic progression (AP) is a list of numbers where each term is the previous term plus a fixed number d, the common difference. d = a₂ − a₁ = a₃ − a₂ = …
d can be positive (growing), negative (shrinking) or zero (constant). 10, 7, 4, 1, … is an AP with d = −3. 1, 4, 9, 16 is not an AP: the differences 3, 5, 7 change.

lessons.aha: AP: every difference a₂ − a₁, a₃ − a₂, … is the same number d.

lessons.title: Jumping straight to the nth term
lessons.story: Anu wants week 20 without writing 20 numbers. Week 1 is 50. To reach week 20, she adds the step 10 nineteen times.
text: The nth term is aₙ = a + (n − 1)d. So a₂₀ = 50 + 19 × 10 = ₹240.
To find which term a number is, solve for n: in 3, 8, 13, …, 78 = 3 + (n − 1)5 gives n = 16. If n is not a positive whole number, the number is not a term of the AP.

lessons.title: Counting from the other end
lessons.story: The AP 3, 8, 13, …, 253 has many terms. 'Find the 20th term from the end,' says Thatha.
text: Reverse the AP: it starts at the last term l = 253 and has common difference −d = −5. So the 20th term from the end = l − (n − 1)d = 253 − 19 × 5 = 158.
Also: the nth term from the end = (m − n + 1)th term from the start, where m is the number of terms.

lessons.title: Same shape, not the same size
lessons.story: Anu looks at a photo and its enlargement. Every angle is the same, but every length is 3 times as long.
text: Two figures are similar if they have the same shape. Two polygons with the same number of sides are similar if (i) their corresponding angles are equal and (ii) their corresponding sides are in the same ratio.
All circles are similar. All squares are similar. All equilateral triangles are similar. Congruent figures are similar with ratio 1, but similar figures need not be congruent.

lessons.title: The Basic Proportionality Theorem
lessons.story: Thatha draws triangle ABC and a line DE parallel to BC. He measures: AD = 2, DB = 3, AE = 2.4, EC = 3.6.
text: 2/3 = 2.4/3.6. Basic Proportionality Theorem (Thales): if a line is drawn parallel to one side of a triangle and meets the other two sides at distinct points, it divides those sides in the same ratio.

Proof idea: join BE and CD. ΔBDE and ΔDEC have the same base DE and lie between the same parallels DE and BC, so their areas are equal. Then ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB and ar(ADE)/ar(DEC) = AE/EC. So AD/DB = AE/EC.

picture.caption: A line parallel to one side divides the other two sides in the same ratio.

think.question: In ΔABC, DE ∥ BC, AD = 1.5 cm, DB = 3 cm, AE = 1 cm. Find EC.

lessons.aha: DE ∥ BC ⇒ AD/DB = AE/EC (also AD/AB = AE/AC).

example.question: Prove the BPT.
steps: Given: in ΔABC, DE ∥ BC, with D on AB and E on AC. To prove: AD/DB = AE/EC.
Construction: join BE and CD. Draw EN ⟂ AB and DM ⟂ AC.
ar(ADE) = ½ × AD × EN and ar(BDE) = ½ × DB × EN, so ar(ADE)/ar(BDE) = AD/DB.
ΔBDE and ΔDEC are on the same base DE and between the same parallels, so ar(BDE) = ar(DEC).

lessons.title: The converse: ratio tells you 'parallel'
lessons.story: Ravi finds a triangle where AD/DB = AE/EC = 2/5. 'Is DE parallel to BC?'
text: Converse of BPT: if a line divides two sides of a triangle in the same ratio, then it is parallel to the third side.
Use it to PROVE that two lines are parallel. Compute both ratios. If they are equal, the line is parallel. If they are not, it is not parallel.

picture.caption: The theorem and its converse swap the given and the result.

lessons.aha: Equal ratios on two sides ⇒ the line is parallel to the third side.

lessons.title: Three quick tests for similarity
lessons.story: Anu does not want to check all 3 angles and all 3 sides every time. Thatha shows three shortcuts.
text: AAA (or AA): if two angles of one triangle equal two angles of the other, the triangles are similar (the third angles are then equal too).

SSS: if all three pairs of sides are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar. SAS: if one angle is equal and the sides including it are in the same ratio, the triangles are similar. Write the vertices in matching order: ΔABC ~ ΔPQR means A ↔ P, B ↔ Q, C ↔ R.

lessons.title: The distance formula
lessons.story: Anu draws the straight path from the school A(1, 1) to the library B(5, 4). Then she draws a right triangle under it: 4 across and 3 up.
text: By Pythagoras, AB² = 4² + 3² = 25, so AB = 5 km. In general, the distance between P(x₁, y₁) and Q(x₂, y₂) is PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
The distance of P(x, y) from the origin is √(x² + y²). The order of subtraction does not matter because we square.

picture.caption: Across 4, up 3, so the distance is 5.

lessons.aha: PQ = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]: Pythagoras on the grid.

lessons.title: Using distances to prove things
lessons.story: Ravi has three points. 'Are they on one straight line? Do they make a right triangle? A square?'
text: Collinear: if AB + BC = AC (the two shorter distances add to the longest), the points lie on one line.

Shapes: equal sides → isosceles or equilateral triangle. Pythagoras → right triangle. Four equal sides and equal diagonals → square. Equidistant point: if P is equidistant from A and B, write PA² = PB² and solve.

lessons.title: The section formula
lessons.story: A rope runs from A(−1, 7) to B(4, −3). Anu ties a ribbon at P, which divides AB in the ratio 2 : 3.
text: P(x, y) divides the segment joining A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) internally in the ratio m₁ : m₂: x = (m₁x₂ + m₂x₁)/(m₁ + m₂), y = (m₁y₂ + m₂y₁)/(m₁ + m₂).
Here x = (2 × 4 + 3 × (−1))/5 = 1 and y = (2 × (−3) + 3 × 7)/5 = 3. So P is (1, 3). Remember: m₁ goes with the far point B.

lessons.title: The mid-point and special cases
lessons.story: The bus stop must be exactly halfway between A(1, 1) and B(5, 4).
text: Mid-point (ratio 1 : 1): ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2) = (3, 2.5).

Trisection points use ratios 1 : 2 and 2 : 1. To find the ratio in which an axis divides AB, take the ratio k : 1: on the x-axis y = 0, on the y-axis x = 0. The diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, so they have the same mid-point. Use this to find a missing vertex.

introduction-trigonometry.intro: Ravi leans a ladder against a wall. 'If I make the ladder steeper, the top goes higher,' he says. Thatha nods. 'The angle decides how the sides of the right triangle compare. Trigonometry gives names to those comparisons.'
before: Pythagoras' theorem
similar triangles have sides in the same ratio
simplify fractions and surds such as √3/2

lessons.title: Naming the sides from the angle
lessons.story: Anu draws a right triangle ABC with ∠B = 90°. She marks the angle A and asks, 'Which side is opposite? Which is next to A?'
text: The hypotenuse AC is the longest side, opposite the right angle. For angle A, the side opposite is BC and the side adjacent (next to A, not the hypotenuse) is AB.
sin A = opposite/hypotenuse = BC/AC, cos A = adjacent/hypotenuse = AB/AC, tan A = opposite/adjacent = BC/AB. The reciprocals are cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A and cot A = 1/tan A.

picture.caption: Opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse are named from angle A.

think.question: In the same triangle, which side is adjacent to angle C?
think.answer: BC (and AB is opposite to C).

lessons.aha: sin = opp/hyp, cos = adj/hyp, tan = opp/adj. Name the sides from the angle you use.
formulas: tan A = opp/adj = sin A/cos A
cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A

lessons.title: The ratio belongs to the angle, not the size
lessons.story: Ravi draws a small ladder triangle and a large one, both with the same angle at the ground.
text: The two right triangles have the same angle A, so they are similar (AA). Their sides are in the same ratio, so BC/AC is the same in both.
That is why sin A depends only on the angle A, not on the size of the triangle. Also, sin A and cos A are always at most 1, because the hypotenuse is the longest side.

picture.caption: Same angle, same ratios, whatever the size.

think.question: Can sin A be 4/3 for some angle A?
think.answer: No. sin A = opp/hyp and the hypotenuse is the longest side, so sin A ≤ 1.

lessons.aha: Trigonometric ratios depend only on the angle. sin A and cos A lie between 0 and 1 for acute angles.

lessons.title: All ratios from one ratio
lessons.story: The question says: 'If tan A = 3/4, find sin A and cos A.' Anu draws a right triangle and labels it.
text: tan A = 3/4 means opposite = 3k and adjacent = 4k. By Pythagoras, hypotenuse = √(9k² + 16k²) = 5k.
So sin A = 3/5 and cos A = 4/5, cosec A = 5/3, sec A = 5/4 and cot A = 4/3. This 'draw the triangle' method works for any one given ratio.

picture.caption: tan A = 3/4 gives the 3-4-5 triangle.

think.question: If sin A = 5/13, find cos A and tan A.
think.answer: Adjacent = 12k, so cos A = 12/13 and tan A = 5/12.

lessons.aha: Given one ratio, draw the triangle, use Pythagoras for the third side, then read every ratio.

lessons.title: Special angles: 45°, 30° and 60°
lessons.story: Thatha cuts a square along its diagonal, and an equilateral triangle down its middle.
text: The half-square is a right triangle with sides 1, 1 and √2. So sin 45° = cos 45° = 1/√2 and tan 45° = 1.
Half an equilateral triangle of side 2 has sides 1, √3 and 2, with angles 30° and 60°. So sin 30° = 1/2, cos 30° = √3/2, tan 30° = 1/√3, sin 60° = √3/2, cos 60° = 1/2 and tan 60° = √3.

picture.caption: Half a square gives 45°. Half an equilateral triangle gives 30° and 60°.

think.question: Find sin 60° cos 30° + sin 30° cos 60°.

lessons.aha: 45°: 1, 1, √2. 30°–60°: 1, √3, 2. Every standard value comes from these two triangles.

lessons.title: The table of values
lessons.story: Anu notices a pattern and writes a small table to remember the standard values.
text: sin goes 0, 1/2, 1/√2, √3/2, 1 as the angle goes 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90°. cos goes the other way. tan = sin/cos, and tan 90° is not defined.

picture.caption: Standard values to know by heart.

think.question: Evaluate 2tan²45° + cos²30° − sin²60°.

lessons.aha: Learn sin values as √0/2, √1/2, √2/2, √3/2, √4/2. cos is the same list reversed. tan = sin/cos.

lessons.title: Identities: true for every angle
lessons.story: Ravi divides Pythagoras' theorem, opp² + adj² = hyp², by hyp². Something nice appears.
text: sin²A + cos²A = 1 for every acute angle A. Dividing by cos²A gives 1 + tan²A = sec²A. Dividing by sin²A gives 1 + cot²A = cosec²A.
To prove an identity, start from the harder side and change it step by step into the other side. Useful moves: write tan and cot as sin/cos, use the three identities, and combine fractions.

picture.caption: Identities come from Pythagoras.

think.question: Prove that (1 − cos²A) cosec²A = 1.

lessons.aha: sin²A + cos²A = 1 is Pythagoras. Prove identities from the harder side towards the simpler side.

formulas: sin A = opp/hyp, cos A = adj/hyp, tan A = opp/adj
cosec A = 1/sin A, sec A = 1/cos A, cot A = 1/tan A
method: Draw a right triangle and mark the angle.
Name opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from that angle.
For values, substitute the standard table.
For identities, start from the harder side and use sin, cos and the three identities.

lessons.title: Angles of elevation and depression
lessons.story: Ravi flies a kite. He looks UP at it. His sister on the balcony looks DOWN at a dog in the garden.
text: The line of sight joins the eye to the object. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when the object is ABOVE the horizontal.
The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and the line of sight when the object is BELOW the horizontal. Both angles are always measured from the horizontal line.

picture.caption: Elevation: look up from the horizontal. Depression: look down from the horizontal.

think.question: A boy on a cliff looks at a boat on the sea. Is this an angle of elevation or depression?
think.answer: Depression: the boat is below the horizontal through his eye.

lessons.aha: Elevation: object above the horizontal. Depression: object below. Measure both from the horizontal.

lessons.title: One right triangle, one unknown
lessons.story: Anu stands 30 m from the tower and sees the top at 60°.
text: The tower, the ground and the line of sight make a right triangle. The known side is adjacent (30 m) and the unknown is opposite (h), so use tan.
tan 60° = h/30, so h = 30√3 m ≈ 51.96 m. Choose the ratio that connects the side you know with the side you want.

picture.caption: Known adjacent, unknown opposite: use tan.

think.question: A kite string is 60 m long and makes 60° with the ground. Find the kite's height.

lessons.aha: Known side and wanted side decide the ratio: opp & adj → tan, opp & hyp → sin, adj & hyp → cos.

lessons.title: Depression becomes elevation
lessons.story: From the top of a 75 m lighthouse, the angle of depression of a ship is 30°. Ravi does not know where to put the 30° in the triangle.
text: The horizontal at the top is parallel to the ground. The line of sight is a transversal. So the angle of depression at the top equals the angle of elevation at the ship (alternate angles).
So put 30° at the ship: tan 30° = 75/d, which gives d = 75√3 m.

picture.caption: Angle of depression = angle of elevation (alternate angles).

think.question: From a 20 m tall building, the angle of depression of a car is 45°. How far is the car?

lessons.aha: Angle of depression from the top = angle of elevation from the bottom object.

lessons.title: Two triangles, one tower
lessons.story: Anu sees the top of a tower at 30°. She walks 40 m towards it and now sees it at 60°.
text: Let the height be h and the second distance be x. In the near triangle: tan 60° = h/x, so h = √3 x. In the far triangle: tan 30° = h/(x + 40), so x + 40 = √3 h = 3x.
So x = 20 m and h = 20√3 m. Two triangles share one side (the tower). Write one equation for each triangle and solve them together.

picture.caption: One tower, two angles: two equations.

think.question: The angles of elevation of a tower from two points 9 m and 4 m from its base, on one side, are complementary. Find the height.
think.answer: tan θ = h/9 and cot θ = h/4, so h² = 36 and h = 6 m.

lessons.aha: Two angles → two triangles → two equations. The common side links them.

circles.intro: Ravi rolls a bicycle wheel along a straight road. 'The wheel touches the road at only one point at a time,' says Anu. 'And the spoke to that point always stands straight up.' The road is a tangent to the wheel, and the spoke is a radius. That one fact solves most questions in this chapter.

congruent triangles (RHS)
Pythagoras' theorem and angle sum of a quadrilateral

lessons.title: A line and a circle: three cases
lessons.story: Anu slides a ruler across a coin. Sometimes the ruler misses the coin, sometimes it touches the edge, and sometimes it cuts across.
text: A line and a circle can have no common point (non-intersecting line), exactly one common point (tangent) or two common points (secant).
The common point of a tangent and the circle is the point of contact. A tangent is a special case of a secant: the two meeting points come together into one.

picture.caption: Non-intersecting line, secant (two points) and tangent (one point).

think.question: How many tangents can a circle have?
think.answer: Infinitely many: one at every point of the circle.

lessons.aha: A tangent meets the circle at exactly one point, the point of contact.

lessons.title: How many tangents from a point?
lessons.story: Thatha marks three points: one inside the circle, one on it and one outside. 'From each point, how many tangents can you draw?'
text: From a point inside the circle: no tangent (every line through it cuts the circle twice).
From a point on the circle: exactly one tangent. From a point outside the circle: exactly two tangents. The length of a tangent is the distance from the outside point to the point of contact.

picture.caption: Tangents through a point.

think.question: Can you draw a tangent to a circle from its centre?
think.answer: No. The centre is inside the circle.

lessons.aha: Inside: 0 tangents. On: 1. Outside: 2.

lessons.title: Theorem 1: the tangent is perpendicular to the radius
lessons.story: Ravi notices that the spoke to the touching point always stands straight up from the road.
text: Theorem: the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.

Proof idea: take any other point Q on the tangent. Q lies outside the circle, so OQ > OP. So OP is the shortest distance from O to the line, and the shortest segment from a point to a line is perpendicular to it.

picture.caption: Every other point Q of the tangent is outside, so OP is the shortest: OP ⟂ tangent.

think.question: A tangent PQ at P meets a line through O at Q. OP = 5 cm and OQ = 12 cm. Find PQ.

lessons.aha: Radius ⟂ tangent at the point of contact. Look for this right angle in every question.

example.question: Prove that the tangent at any point of a circle is perpendicular to the radius through the point of contact.
steps: Given: a circle with centre O and a tangent XY at P. To prove: OP ⟂ XY.
Take any point Q on XY other than P and join OQ.
Q lies outside the circle (a tangent meets the circle only at P), so OQ > OP.
This is true for every point Q on XY except P, so OP is the shortest distance from O to XY.
The shortest segment from a point to a line is the perpendicular. So OP ⟂ XY.

lessons.title: Theorem 2: two tangents from outside are equal
lessons.story: From a point P outside the circle, Anu draws two tangents PQ and PR. She measures them: both are 7.2 cm.
text: Theorem: the lengths of the tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
Proof: join OQ, OR and OP. ∠OQP = ∠ORP = 90° (Theorem 1), OQ = OR (radii) and OP is common. So ΔOQP ≅ ΔORP (RHS), and PQ = PR. The same congruence also shows that OP bisects ∠QPR.

picture.caption: Tangents from an external point are equal: PQ = PR.

think.question: Tangents PA and PB from P make ∠APB = 70°. Find ∠AOB.

lessons.aha: Two tangents from one outside point are equal (RHS congruence).

example.question: Prove that the lengths of the tangents drawn from an external point to a circle are equal.
steps: Given: a circle with centre O, and tangents PQ and PR from an external point P. To prove: PQ = PR.

lessons.title: Using the two theorems
lessons.story: Thatha draws a quadrilateral ABCD whose four sides all touch one circle.
text: Each vertex sends two equal tangents. Adding them gives AB + CD = AD + BC. This is a favourite board proof.

Two more uses: (1) With tangents PA and PB, ∠APB + ∠AOB = 180°. (2) For two concentric circles, a chord of the bigger circle that touches the smaller circle is bisected at the point of contact, so its length is 2√(R² − r²).

areas-circles.intro: Anu's family orders a round pizza of radius 21 cm and cuts it into 6 equal slices. 'Each slice is a sector,' says Thatha. 'How much pizza is in one slice? And how long is the crust on it?' Areas and lengths of parts of a circle answer these everyday questions.

lessons.title: Circle facts and wheels
lessons.story: Ravi's bicycle wheel has a radius of 35 cm. 'How far does it go in one turn?'
text: In one turn the wheel covers its circumference: 2πr = 2 × 22/7 × 35 = 220 cm. In n turns it covers n × 2πr.
Area of a circle = πr². The area between two concentric circles (a ring) = π(R² − r²).

picture.caption: Basic circle formulas.

think.question: How many turns does a wheel of radius 35 cm make to cover 1.1 km?

lessons.aha: One turn of a wheel = one circumference.

lessons.title: Sectors and arcs: a fraction of the circle
lessons.story: Each pizza slice has an angle of 360° ÷ 6 = 60° at the centre.
text: A sector with angle θ is θ/360 of the whole circle. So area of sector = (θ/360) × πr², and length of arc = (θ/360) × 2πr.
For the pizza: area = (60/360) × 22/7 × 21 × 21 = 231 cm² and crust (arc) = (60/360) × 2 × 22/7 × 21 = 22 cm. The larger part of the circle is the major sector, with angle 360° − θ.

picture.caption: A sector is a 'pizza slice': θ/360 of the circle.

think.question: Find the area of a sector of radius 4 cm and angle 30° (π = 3.14).

lessons.aha: Sector = θ/360 of the area. Arc = θ/360 of the circumference.
formulas: Area of major sector = πr² − area of minor sector

lessons.title: Segment = sector − triangle
lessons.story: Anu cuts a chord across the pizza. The piece between the chord and the crust is a segment.
text: Area of minor segment = area of sector − area of the triangle formed by the two radii and the chord.
For θ = 90°: triangle area = ½r². For θ = 60°: the triangle is equilateral, area = (√3/4)r². The board syllabus uses only these two angles for segments.

picture.caption: Segment (gold) = sector OAB − triangle OAB.

surface-areas-volumes.intro: At the fair, Anu sees a circus tent: a cylinder at the bottom with a cone on top. 'How much canvas did they need?' she wonders. Ravi holds an ice-cream cone with a half-ball of ice cream on top. 'And how much ice cream is in this?' Many real objects are made by joining two simple solids.

lessons.title: The basic solids
lessons.story: Before joining solids, Thatha asks Anu to list the formulas for each one.
text: Curved surface area (CSA) is the area of the curved part only. Total surface area (TSA) includes the flat faces too. Volume is the space inside.
For a cone, the slant height l = √(r² + h²). A hemisphere has CSA 2πr² and TSA 3πr² (curved part plus the flat circle).

picture.caption: The formulas you need for combined solids.

think.question: A cone has r = 3 cm and h = 4 cm. Find its slant height.

lessons.aha: Know CSA, TSA and volume for each basic solid. Cone: l² = r² + h².

lessons.title: Surface area of a combined solid: count only what you can touch
lessons.story: The circus tent is a cylinder of radius 14 m and height 3 m with a cone of slant height 25 m on top. The tent has no floor.
text: When two solids are joined, the faces where they meet are hidden. So surface area of the combination = sum of the visible surfaces only, NOT the sum of the two TSAs.
Tent canvas = CSA of cylinder + CSA of cone = 2π(14)(3) + π(14)(25) = 264 + 1,100 = 1,364 m².

picture.caption: Only the outside surfaces count. The joined faces are hidden.

think.question: A toy is a cone on a hemisphere, both of radius 3.5 cm. The total height is 15.5 cm. Which surfaces make its total surface area?

lessons.aha: Surface area of a combined solid = sum of the visible curved and flat parts.

lessons.title: Volume of a combined solid: add or subtract
lessons.story: Ravi's ice cream is a cone (r = 3 cm, h = 10 cm) with a hemisphere of ice cream on top.
text: Volumes simply add when solids are joined: ⅓πr²h + (2/3)πr³ = ⅓π(9)(10) + (2/3)π(27) = 30π + 18π = 48π cm³.
When a solid is scooped out (for example, a pen stand with holes, or a cylinder with conical hollows), subtract the volume of the removed parts.

lines: Surface may GAIN inner curved parts

picture.caption: Volumes add or subtract. Surfaces need care.

lessons.aha: Joined: add volumes. Removed: subtract volumes. Surface area is never just 'add the TSAs'.

statistics.intro: Forty students took a 50-mark test. The teacher puts the marks into groups: 0–10, 10–20, and so on. 'What is a typical score?' asks Anu. 'The mean, median and mode each answer that question in a different way,' says Thatha. In this chapter all three use the same class data: frequencies 5, 8, 15, 7, 5.

lessons.title: Class marks: one number for each class
lessons.story: Anu cannot see the exact marks inside the class 20–30. Thatha says, 'Assume every mark is at the centre of its class.'
text: The class mark (mid-point) of a class is xᵢ = (lower limit + upper limit)/2. For 20–30, xᵢ = 25.
In 'continuous' classes like 10–20, 20–30, a score of exactly 20 goes into 20–30 (the upper class). If classes are like 10–19, 20–29, first make them continuous (9.5–19.5, 19.5–29.5).

picture.caption: Class marks are the mid-points of the classes.

lessons.aha: Class mark xᵢ = (lower + upper)/2. It stands for every value in that class.

lessons.title: Mean by the direct method
lessons.story: Anu multiplies each class mark by its frequency and adds.
text: Mean x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ. Make columns fᵢ, xᵢ and fᵢxᵢ.
Here Σfᵢ = 40 and Σfᵢxᵢ = 990, so x̄ = 990/40 = 24.75.

picture.caption: Direct method: x̄ = 990/40 = 24.75.

think.question: If Σfᵢ = 50 and Σfᵢxᵢ = 1,320, find the mean.

lessons.aha: Direct method: x̄ = Σfᵢxᵢ / Σfᵢ.

lessons.title: Shortcuts: assumed mean and step deviation
lessons.story: The class marks were big numbers. Ravi wants smaller numbers to multiply.
text: Assumed mean method: choose a = a middle class mark (25). Let dᵢ = xᵢ − a. Then x̄ = a + Σfᵢdᵢ/Σfᵢ = 25 + (−10)/40 = 24.75.
Step-deviation method: also divide by the class width h = 10: uᵢ = (xᵢ − a)/h. Then x̄ = a + h × Σfᵢuᵢ/Σfᵢ = 25 + 10 × (−1/40) = 24.75. All three methods give the same mean.

think.question: With a = 50, h = 10, Σfᵢuᵢ = 12 and Σfᵢ = 60, find the mean.

lessons.aha: Assumed mean: x̄ = a + Σfd/Σf. Step deviation: x̄ = a + h × Σfu/Σf.

lessons.title: Mode: the tallest bar
lessons.story: Ravi draws a histogram. The tallest bar is the class 20–30 (frequency 15). That is the modal class.
text: Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h. Here l = 20 (lower limit of the modal class), f₁ = 15 (its frequency), f₀ = 8 (class before), f₂ = 7 (class after), h = 10.
Mode = 20 + (7/15) × 10 = 20 + 4.67 = 24.67. The formula moves the mode towards the taller neighbour.

picture.caption: The modal class 20–30 has the highest frequency.

think.question: In the formula for the mode, what is f₀?
think.answer: The frequency of the class just before the modal class.

lessons.aha: Find the modal class (highest f), then Mode = l + (f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂) × h.
formulas: Mode = l + [(f₁ − f₀)/(2f₁ − f₀ − f₂)] × h

lessons.title: Median: the middle student
lessons.story: Anu lines up all 40 students by marks. The median is the mark of the student in the middle, at n/2 = 20.
text: Make a cumulative frequency (cf) column: 5, 13, 28, 35, 40. The first cf that reaches 20 is 28, so the median class is 20–30.
Median = l + [(n/2 − cf)/f] × h, where cf is the cumulative frequency of the class BEFORE the median class. Median = 20 + [(20 − 13)/15] × 10 = 24.67.

picture.caption: n/2 = 20 falls in 20–30, the median class.

think.question: n = 60. The cf column is 8, 20, 35, 50, 60. Which is the median class?
think.answer: n/2 = 30, the first cf ≥ 30 is 35: the third class.

lessons.aha: Find n/2, then the median class from the cf column. Median = l + (n/2 − cf)/f × h.

lessons.title: Mean, median and mode together
lessons.story: Anu got mean 24.75, median 24.67 and mode 24.67. 'They are close!' she says.
text: For moderately symmetric data, the three measures are related: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean (empirical relationship).
Use it to find one measure when two are given. Check: 3 × 24.67 = 74.0 and 24.67 + 2 × 24.75 = 74.17, which is nearly equal.

picture.caption: The empirical relationship.

lessons.aha: 3 Median = Mode + 2 Mean.

probability.intro: Before the cricket match, the captains toss a coin. 'Heads or tails: each has an equal chance,' says Ravi. Later, Anu plays a board game with two dice and hopes for a total of 7. 'Is 7 more likely than 12?' Probability measures how likely an event is, as a number from 0 to 1.

lessons.title: Probability as a fraction
lessons.story: Anu puts 3 red balls and 5 blue balls in a bag and draws one without looking. Each ball has an equal chance.
text: When all outcomes are equally likely, P(E) = (number of outcomes favourable to E) / (total number of outcomes).
So P(red) = 3/8 and P(blue) = 5/8. The words 'at random' or 'well-shuffled' tell you that the outcomes are equally likely.

picture.caption: Every probability lies between 0 and 1.

think.question: A die is thrown once. Find P(a number greater than 4).

lessons.aha: $P(E)=\dfrac{\text{favourable outcomes}}{\text{total outcomes}}$, when all outcomes are equally likely.

lessons.title: Sure, impossible and 'not E'
lessons.story: Ravi throws a die. 'What is the chance of getting 7?' Anu laughs: 'Zero!'
text: An impossible event has probability 0. A sure event has probability 1. So 0 ≤ P(E) ≤ 1 for every event.
The event 'not E' (written Ē) happens exactly when E does not happen. P(E) + P(not E) = 1. For a die, P(not 6) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6.

picture.caption: The probabilities of an event and its complement add to 1.

think.question: If P(E) = 0.05, find P(not E).

lessons.aha: P(not E) = 1 − P(E). Impossible: 0. Sure: 1.

lessons.title: Tossing coins
lessons.story: Two coins are tossed together. Ravi says, 'There are 3 outcomes: two heads, two tails, one of each.' Thatha says, 'Careful!'
text: List the outcomes in order: HH, HT, TH, TT. There are 4 equally likely outcomes, not 3. 'One head and one tail' happens in 2 ways (HT and TH).
So P(exactly one head) = 2/4 = 1/2 and P(at least one head) = 3/4. For three coins there are 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 outcomes.

picture.caption: Two coins give 4 equally likely outcomes.

think.question: Three coins are tossed. Find P(all heads).

lessons.aha: List ordered outcomes. Two coins: 4 outcomes. Three coins: 8.

lessons.title: Two dice: 36 outcomes
lessons.story: Anu throws two dice. She draws a 6 × 6 table of sums.
text: There are 6 × 6 = 36 equally likely outcomes. A sum of 7 happens in 6 ways: (1, 6), (2, 5), (3, 4), (4, 3), (5, 2), (6, 1). So P(sum 7) = 6/36 = 1/6.
A sum of 12 happens in only 1 way, (6, 6), so P(sum 12) = 1/36. Doublets (same number on both) happen in 6 ways: P = 1/6.

picture.caption: The 36 sums. A total of 7 appears 6 times.

There are 26 red and 26 black cards, 4 aces, 4 kings, and 12 face cards (J, Q, K). So P(king) = 4/52 = 1/13, P(face card) = 12/52 = 3/13 and P(red king) = 2/52 = 1/26.
